answer: Each boat that passes the lock is written in the keeper's gate book, and the keeper signs the entry before the gates may open again. A inlet boat that slips through at night fails the book: at the lantern of the passage the water level must match the keeper's own mark, and a night boat leaves the gates unlogged. Buying a false passage means bribing the keeper, forging a year of entries and paying 15,200, while the relic signature in the gate book is read at every inspection, so a boat whose passage was never logged is seized at the next lock.
